GOSS retains large-gradient examples and subsamples small-gradient ones with reweighting, targeting examples that strongly influence split gain. EFB bundles sparse, nearly mutually exclusive features to reduce effective dimensionality. Leaf-wise growth splits the currently most promising leaf; depth-wise growth expands a level more uniformly. [1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/6449f44a102fde848669bdd9eb6b76fa-Abstract.html)

Best-first growth can reduce training loss with fewer leaves but may create deep, specialized branches and overfit small datasets. Limit leaves, depth, and minimum leaf data. XGBoost also supports multiple growth/histogram strategies, so “LightGBM leaf-wise, XGBoost always depth-wise” is outdated as a universal distinction. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02754)

Compare actual configurations, categorical handling, memory, training time, and held-out quality. Neither GOSS nor EFB guarantees a speedup or quality match on dense or highly interacting features.
